extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and practitioners in linguistics and humor studies (people analyzing or studying verbal humor)
extracted.subtask_description: Use linguistic-semantic criteria (script theory, SSTH, GTVH) to analyze or evaluate verbal jokes and humorous texts, focusing on script overlap/opposition, logical mechanisms, narrative strategy, target, situation, and language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script-based Semantic Theory (general semantic framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Meaning is characterized as a semantic graph (network) of scripts (nodes) and labeled links (edges such as ISA, part-of, agent). The meaning of words/sentences is given by the set of links of the relevant script(s) and by disambiguation driven by context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use script networks to represent lexical and situational knowledge; disambiguation proceeds by discarding alternative script senses under contextual pressure (e.g., 'apple' as FRUIT vs. company). This framework informs how competing script activations arise in texts and enables mapping lexical items into semantic domains for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script-based Semantic Theory of Humor (SSTH)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor arises when a text is compatible with two distinct and opposing semantic scripts; a 'script' is a cognitive structure encoding stereotypical information about situations, participants, actions, goals, and sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To judge whether a text is humorous under SSTH, check (1) compatibility with two different scripts and (2) that those scripts stand in opposition. The theory expects a setup that activates one script and a punchline that makes a second, conflicting script plausible, producing incongruity and reinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script Overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: The text is compatible with two different semantic scripts (sets of expectations or knowledge about a situation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the scripts activated by parts of the text; overlap occurs when the same text can be interpreted under two script schemas. Overlap is necessary but not sufficient for humor; document which script elements (participants, actions, goals) align with each interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script Opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The two scripts compatible with the text are in clear opposition (examples: real vs. unreal; normal vs. abnormal; life vs. death; good vs. bad; high vs. low; literal vs. non-literal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the simultaneous applicability of two scripts creates a semantic clash—opposition should be clear and salient (e.g., professional vs. illicit). Use the listed common oppositions as diagnostic categories when analyzing a joke's semantic conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism of humor: setup → punchline → reinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Most jokes follow a setup that activates Script A and a punchline that introduces Script B; the punchline triggers reinterpretation by revealing an alternative meaning that resolves the incongruity between the scripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a joke, trace how the setup leads the hearer to adopt Script A, where cues are placed, and how the punchline forces switching to Script B. The humorous effect depends on the hearer recognizing the second script and resolving the conflict. Example analysis steps: (1) identify setup script, (2) identify punchline-triggered script, (3) show the reinterpretation and the source of incongruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplar analysis: 'Is the Doctor at Home?'
rubrics_metrics.description: A canonical textbook exemplar used to teach script-based analysis: setup (sick patient seeking help) suggests a medical script; punchline ('No. Come right in.') reveals an adultery/affair script, producing humor via opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this short joke as a teaching example: enumerate the scripts activated by the setup and punchline; specify the opposition (Professional/Medical visit vs. Illicit/Romantic affair) and how the punchline forces reinterpretation. Note the exemplar status: simple, average, and reflecting historical source stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-bona fide communication (pragmatic mode criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor operates in a non-bona fide mode in which cooperative conversational maxims (truthfulness, informativeness, relevance, clarity) are suspended or flouted; a joke is 'a bona fide non-bona fide text'—the hearer initially treats it as sincere then recognizes purposeful deviation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the text contains cues prompting the hearer to switch from bona fide to non-bona fide interpretation (often at or near the punchline). Analysis should track: (1) initial processing as bona fide, (2) the cue revealing need for non-bona fide reinterpretation, (3) reconstruction of meaning under the alternative script. Look for intentional violations of Gricean maxims.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Theory of Verbal Humor (GTVH) — Knowledge Resources (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: GTVH supplements SSTH by identifying six semi-independent Knowledge Resources (KRs) that structure verbal humor: Script Opposition (SO), Logical Mechanism (LM), Situation (SI), Target (TA), Narrative Strategy (NS), Language (LG).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the six KRs as an analytic rubric to classify and compare jokes: some resources (SO, LM) constrain the core of the joke; others (NS, LG, TA, SI) can be varied to produce different surface realizations. The KRs operate semi-independently and can be manipulated to generate joke variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical Mechanism (LM)
rubrics_metrics.description: The technique that connects the scripts (e.g., a pun, faulty logic, misdirection) and provides the inferential link producing the switch between scripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the LM used in the joke (e.g., pun, equivocation, false inference, analogical transfer). Assess its role in enabling the reinterpretation: does the LM plausibly connect Script A and Script B, and is it executed clearly enough for the audience to perform the switch?

rubrics_metrics.name: Situation (SI)
rubrics_metrics.description: The setting or contextual circumstances of the joke (where and when the event is situated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the situational parameters that frame possible script activations (locations, social roles, activities). Situational cues feed script activation and shape which oppositions are salient; changing SI can alter perceived humor or applicability of scripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target (TA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The entity that is the focus of the humor (who or what is being ridiculed, criticized, or otherwise targeted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the joke targets individuals, social groups, institutions, concepts, or none (purely situational). Analysis should consider how the target interacts with scripts and whether targeting affects acceptability, punchline force, or ethical evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative Strategy (NS)
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure and delivery of the joke (e.g., simple narrative, dialogue, riddle, one-liner) that organizes how the script opposition and logical mechanism are revealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify the narrative strategy and assess its effect on timing, cue placement, and audience processing. Variations in NS (e.g., presentational order, use of characters) can change comedic impact even when other KRs are held constant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language (LG)
rubrics_metrics.description: The linguistic form and style used (wording, register, prosody, rhetorical devices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine lexical choices, syntactic structure, ambiguity, phonological features (for puns), and register shifts. Language can instantiate or obscure scripts and the logical mechanism; small linguistic changes can produce different humorous outcomes.
